query: Why should I consider using trekking poles for hiking, especially if I'm not looking to spend a lot? I’ve been hesitant about them but have heard they could really help with my hiking stamina and knee pain. What features should I look for in affordable poles, and how can I ensure I'm using them correctly to avoid issues?
ori_review:
My husband and I have been avid hikers over the past 15 years. But we poo-pood trekking poles. I would see other hikers slide using them and thought they would just get in the way.
This spring we were getting ready to complete the ADK Firetower Challenge. We needed to hike 5 mountains in 6 days. I joined a Facebook group about these hikes. And that is where I realized trekking poles would be beneficial. We didn’t want to spend a lot of money on poles that would only get used 5-10 times a year. Someone in the group recommended these. As soon as I read Ken and Cathy’s review (after laughing so hard), I knew if they liked the poles, so would we.
Well, they are the best! And I will never hike without them again. We have used them on trails that were dry, wet, snow covered, and even ice. Through mud and creeks. I feel they help my cardio stamina going up trails. And oh man, the difference in my knees going down! Worth every penny. Now I did watch a ton of you tube videos on how to measure for best height. And where to position them when going up or down mountains. . Just like when I was learning the best way to kayak, I found just do what works for you. When I had the poles at the height recommended going down mountains, my knees still hurt. When I raised them higher, that was my magic spot! So experiment with height and placement. These poles have kept me from sliding on my tush quite a few times. And at 66, I’m doing all I can to avoid falling.
I love these poles so much, when I saw them at an even cheaper price than I paid for them earlier this year, I bought another pair. Same color.
READ THE DIRECTIONS! I am quite confident that any of the negative reviews were due to user error.
Open the latch before tightening them. Check the latch before each use. I have had to tighten them on occasion. I put my full weight on each pole to test before use, and have never had the pole collapse on me. They fold up nicely to a manageable size when not in use. I love that it comes with extra tip, and accessories for mud, and snow.
There is no need to spend a fortune on trekking poles. We ran into a retired mountain hiking tour guide on one of our hikes. He and his friend both were using these poles. He said in all of his years as a tour guide, he tried several poles, and found the Trail Buddy to be the best.
Do not hesitate to buy these. You won’t regret it.

query: I'm looking for a switch that has a bright indicator light but I need it to have consistent brightness across multiple units. I've noticed some switches have varying brightness due to the resistor placement, and I want to ensure that all my switches can be adjusted to match in brightness. Additionally, I want to modify the wiring so that the indicator light only turns on during the momentary on position, rather than when the switch is in the steady on position. Can you help me find a waterproof option that can withstand salt spray, especially for the internal components? I need it to pass inspection as well.
ori_review: Nice bright indicator light. I bought eight of these and in some of them the resistor was inside the switch on the negative side of the LED and strangely that made those ones brighter. I was able to move the spring and resistor matching the rest so that all of my switches were the same brightness. I also had to move the positive wire of the LED to only the momentary terminal so that my light only lit up when the pump had power.  The way they have the switch lit is so the light is on when it's in the on position and the light is also on when you're holding the switch in the momentary on position. But because of the way my system is wired I had to open the switch and move the positive leg of the LED so the light only came on when it was in the momentary on position, this way when it is in the steady on position the light was back fed through the system so the light would only come on when the automatic float came up that way we knew when the automatic system was pumping due to high water.  After this alteration it passes Coast Guard inspection. Only the outside of the switch is waterproof and actually has a o-ring on The Rocker to prevent water entry. The switch body underneath the dash and the terminals are not waterproof so if you have salt spray back there it will rot out the internals of the switch.

ori_review:
I wanted a mini pedal exerciser for a few months now; something that I could use while I'm watching TV, so I don't feel like I'm being so lazy and so I could get some exercise and multitask.

I was initially looking at the more expensive types that were over $100 and had a lot more plastic. But then I noticed these less expensive and simpler ones that seemed like there weren't as many plastic parts that could potentially break. Some of the less expensive models didn't have displays / counters, but this one did, it was cheap enough and the reviews were good enough so I took a chance and bought one. I've only had it for 4 or 5 days but I'm so happy with it!

The display tracks calories burned, revolutions and time pedaled and I couldn't be happier. It works well, it came already assembled (battery included), it has adjustable tension, and it folds up. It comes with a strap to attach to a chair so it doesn't slide, but I put mine on the floor in front of the couch on my living room carpet and it doesn't slide at all.

It's pretty quiet and the sound from the TV covers up any small noises that it does make. One of the pedal straps (stirrups) is a little bit bent and hits the metal bar that the pedal is attached to, so it makes a tiny tapping sound, but I'm sure I can get the stirrup eventually to bend away so that doesn't happen. That noise is not a deal-breaker for me though. It's very quiet. The stirrups can be adjusted so if I move it to a different hole, that tapping would probably stop, but I haven't tried to move the stirrup yet because I'm afraid I'll break it since the stirrup plastic is a bit rigid.

All in all, I am completely happy with this purchase and if anything does eventually go wrong with the exerciser, I will update my review at that time. But right now I would say to definitely buy one if you want a simple way to exercise while watching TV!

query: I'm looking for an easy and cost-effective way to regrip my golf clubs. I've had my clubs for around 10 years, and the grips are in bad shape. Can you guide me on how to use a grip kit effectively, including what additional supplies I might need, like solvent, and any tips for the regripping process? I want to ensure I do it right and have a good experience when playing with the new grips.
ori_review:
I'm not one of those golfers that buy a new set of clubs every year or so, and, after 10 years, the grips on my clubs were in bad shape. I purchased the Golf Pride kit and was able to completely re-grip my set of clubs in a couple of hours. The kit contains 13 grips (you need a different kind of grip for your putter), grip tape and a rubber vice grip (so you won't scratch your club when placing it in a vice). It does not include the grip solvent, which I purchased at a local golf shop earlier when I re-gripped my putter. The instructions tell you about other solvents you can use that can be purchased in a hardware store.

The process is easy:
- Remove the old grip and tape (I used a utility knife but be careful not to scratch the shaft) - be sure all the old tape is removed;
- Place the rubber vice grip on the shaft and place the club in the vice;
- Remove the plastic label from the new grip;
- Apply the tape to the end of the shaft, leaving about 1/4 inch or so overlap on the end (it makes it easier to start the grip on the shaft). The tape is double-sided, so you peel off one side, apply it to the shaft, and then peel off the other side;
- Apply the solvent to the tape - I just applied it to the top and used a finger to spread it out. This makes the tape slippery, activating the glue. Use plenty of solvent so the tape is very slippery.
- Place some solvent inside the grip itself and be sure the inside is coated;
- Finally, with the grip's label where you want it, slide the grip on the tape until it's completely on the club. You have a few seconds to position the logo as you want it.
- Set the club on the floor grip down to drain any solvent that might be remaining.

That's all there is to it. I played a round the next day with new grips and it felt great.

query: I'm looking for tips on how to successfully use a refillable hand warmer, specifically regarding the lighting process. I've noticed some negative reviews about difficulty in getting the burner to light properly. How can I ensure that I’m following the correct steps and giving it enough time to work effectively? Any advice on the initial lighting and how to maintain it would be greatly appreciated!
ori_review:
I see a lot of negative reviews for this thing. The problem I think is their lack of patience with a new burner. I purchased this and a spare burner, because they do eventually go out (though it takes a long while) and having a backup for when that happens is nice. My first thought about why so many negative reviews exist for this thing is lack of patience and not heeding the instructions. After pouring the lighter fluid inside the little tank WITHOUT the burner on, replace the burner and the cap and let it sit upright for about two minutes. This lets the fluid vapor finish soaking through the cotton and padding and allow the fumes to lightly saturate the catalyst in the burner. The burner isn't going light right if you don't give it a few minutes EVERY. TIME. YOU FILL IT.

And yet still, on first light (maybe even the second light) with a brand new burner, the burner doesn't play nice. You have to apply that flame for a good 10 or more seconds like the instructions say. (If you're doing it at night or in the dark, the orange glow from the catalyst shows it's lit. If you're lighting during the day time, find a dark corner or cup your hand round the cap and look through the holes, you should see something that resembles an ember despite the daylight) After the burner has gone through roughly an hour of burning (and perhaps even less than that) from then on the catalyst lights very quickly and stays hot for the full 12 hours that it should. You just gotta break the little fella in; I have two now.

query: I'm looking for a tactical belt that offers good value for money, ideally around $25. I want something that is well-built and comfortable, but I have some concerns about the molly system being too loose and the Velcro not matching industry standards. Can I expect this belt to hold up well under a load of 15-20 lbs, and will it work well with other magazine pouches I might want to use in the future? Also, how does it compare to more expensive options?
ori_review:
So let me start by saying this a an AMAZING BELT FOR THE MONEY!!! If you're looking for a CHEAP and for the money an amazing deal. Buy with confidence after you read the pros and cons to see if its right for you.

That said a 25 dollar belt is NOT going to stack well against 150-250 belt systems. I will try to get photos of my Ronin Tactical belt and compare it directly to this belt. It doesn't stack up amazingly. But for shooters or airsofters who want a well built belt but are restricted by income this is a great option.

Pros:

Its a tactical belt for 25 bucks! And it doesn't fall apart as soon as you lock it.

Inner belt webbing is comfortable with a soft grip so it won't rotate on you.

Seems to be built extremely well for the money.

Has a Cobra Locking System.

Double or maybe Triple stitched is most areas.

Love to help out an American Veteran anytime I can.

CONS:
Has 2 major ones in my book.

The molly system is too loose from top, middle, and bottom. The molly system is also too soft and not ridged enough. What does this mean? When you web in single magazine pouches there is quite a bit of play side to side. Which feeds to the second issue.

By having loose molly webbing it will cause a weighted magazine pouch to pull the already too loose webbing forward. I believe this over the long term will cause issues. This is my option

Another gripe from me is the Velcro is not industry norm. In the tactical belt or war belt community the outer belt has male Velcro and the inner belt is female Velcro. I have 2 other battle belts, and wanted to try this belt with a inner belt fed through my belt loops. Because the Velcro isn't industry norm it would be female (soft Velcro side) on female.

Finally I wouldn't want more than 15-20LBS on this belt. But this goes for all warbelts that don't have a locking inner belt.

Final Thoughts:

Mission dictates gear. I can't help new shooters with this enough. With the Cons above how am I giving this 5 stars?!? Because I can live with the cons from a 25 dollar warbelt. I had some extra mag pouches and wanted to make a truck belt that if it got stolen I wouldn't cry about it. I can also let friends borrow this when shooting for fun drills. This belt is amazing for the price.

If you are restricted by funds I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this belt. I would recommend buying name brand magazine pouches. So if you do step up from this belt in the future you don't need to purchase higher quality mag pouches.

I will be uploading photos and a video review shortly.

The powder did it's job. other people have mentioned similar products you can find at RV supply stores I'm not sure if there is a cheaper more generic bulk product that might be less expensive if you use this regularly, but for my trip this package was more than enough I could have probably used half given the wag bags already started with some in them. They don’t sell the 48v 30ah controller on Amazon, but if you email them when u make your purchase, you can upgrade. And I strongly urge you to.
48v 30ah has to be experienced to believe!!

Matter of fact, 48v 30ah controller is so much better than 48v 22 ah that comes with order (which definitely ain’t bad) that I ordered a second set and paid full price for upgraded controller and display ($139 + $20 upgrade fee) to have when I build/mod my next ebike.

query: I'm looking for a stable inflatable paddle board that can handle ocean use, especially in choppy water. I want something that's easy to pump up and store, suitable for both my 12-year-old and myself. It should come with good accessories, like a leash and a carrying strap, and I need it to be durable enough for frequent use. Can you recommend a board that matches these needs and has a good reputation for quality?
ori_review:
For reference, I bought this for frequent ocean use. I live on a tropical island and already own to solid boards: one Naish and one Vesl. Both of those boards, the Vesl in particular, are high quality. The boards are primarily used within a lagoon where water is fairly calm, though we also use our SUPs for easy surfing when swells are there. My 12-yr old loves the Vesl but that's also my favorite so I went searching for inflatables as something he can use. After reading a lot of reviews and looking for something with the same dimensions as my Vesl (shorter and wider than the Naish for more stability), I settled on the Roc. I bought it from Amazon Warehouse so it was a bit of a gamble.

Out of the box, it looked unused and all components were present. I used the included pump and timed myself. 5 1/2 minutes continuous, though easy pumping without trying to "race". Definitely broke a sweat but it wasn't difficult to pump up at all. Please note (and this may be obvious already): the gauge will not register psi until the board appears mostly inflated. From there (5 psi), the pumping gets a little more difficult but goes quick. I stopped at 12 psi since I knew this would always be used in the hot sun. After pumping it, I stored it for 4 days to check for any leaks. Still registers at 12 psi after that.

I left this inflated and strapped it to the top of my car, along with one of my solid boards. 15' straps were perfect for this set up. If you were strapping two inflatable SUPs to the top, you'd need 20' straps since the inflatables are thicker than the solids. This is also pretty small once collapsed and stored in the included bag, so it wouldn't be difficult to set it up at the beach.

First impressions in somewhat choppy water with a strong current (both from a distant tropical storm): this board is stable and cuts through the water fairly quick. Had no trouble staying together between this board and the Vesl. It definitely feels a little different...not squishy per se, but just not the same as a solid board. The foam grip pad is great, the handle works well and isn't bothersome, the straps and D-rings are fantastic inclusions for this board. The paddle feels heavy compared to my carbon fiber paddle, but the cool thing is that it adjusts to a lower height than my other one, so my 12-yr old can use this with a proper fit. I also like that it initially floats. It doesn't stay floating, but it doesn't need to--you have enough time to pluck it from the water if you fall off.

I appreciated that this came with everything right out of the box. The leash is of good quality and looks nearly identical to my coiled Dakine leash. There was an included carrying strap for the board, once inflated, in case someone needs to carry it far down a beach or anything. The backpack/duffel is impressively well constructed. The fin is easy to attach and detach, and you get a high quality small dry bag (looks just like my expensive ScubaPro one) for phone, keys, etc. All in all...I am super impressed. Time will tell how it holds up, but I'm surprised what it comes with at this price point. Great board to learn on, nice and stable, would be great for SUP yoga as well.

I'm a smidgin under 5' 11" and this is good for me at the tallest seat setting. My criterion is that the knee should be almost straight at the bottom of the pedal stroke. It also works for me wife, who is 5'0" -- just barely. That's a big range of adjustment -- far greater than what most similar machines offer. I had to send back a competing brand's unit because it was too small. My knees never got close to straight.

It is really, really sturdy and smooth pedaling. Quiet. Good seat. Great to have a backrest. It's super that the seat angle is adjustable -- many similar machines lack the seat angle adjustment feature. Really well designed and well made.

I researched this purchase very hard. I'm fussy about fit and quality. I recommend this machine.

Assembly instructions could be a little better, but they were good enough. The weakest part of the instructions is stpe 10 on page 9 "Resistance Band Assembly." I couldn't tell what they were talking about and did it wrong the first time. Here is what it should say:

"Find the pulley assemblies that are on the resistance bands. The resistance bands are the stretchy cords for hand and arm exercise. The pulleys will have slid down along the resistance bands to the point where they are even with the big black knob for adjusting pedaling resistance,but on the opposite side of the frame (the side away from you are sitting on the seat. The pulleys need to be brought up and bolted to the brackets just below the handlebars, that face you when you are on the seat. Remove the two bolts from the bracket, put the hole in the pulley between the ears of the bracket, and put each bol through the bracket and the pulley. Put on the nuts. You will need to relieve the tension on the resistance bands in order to t do this. Have an assistant grasp the bands below the pulleys and stretch the bands upward and hold them so that the top part of the bands that you are working with when trying to bolt on the pulleys are not under tension while you line them up with the holes in the bracket and put the bolts in."

The key part of the above is that there ARE pulleys on the elastic bands and they will have slid down where you won't notice them

query: I'm looking for a small, adjustable focus LED flashlight that uses AAA batteries. I want something bright but don't necessarily need multiple brightness settings. I've seen some flashlights that have zoom features, but I’m curious if this one also allows for easy zooming. I’ve read mixed things about the brightness levels and whether they truly change, so I’d like to know more about its performance and if it’s reliable for regular use.
ori_review:
I've got about a dozen LED flashlights - most bought that way and some are retrofits (a Maglite, a Rayovac, and a 1st gen SnakeLight). They vary in brightness from 30 or so lumens up to 800 lumens. My favorite is my EDC (every day carry) Mini MLR2 that's 1/2 inch shorter than my chapstick and has 7 settings, including a high setting of 180 lumens. I'm currently jonesin' for a $120 L3 K40 with 1147 lumens and 700 meter beam distance - that thing is FRIGGIN' AWESOME! Now, I'm no flashaholic . . . ok - scratch that. I guess my point is that even though I didn't need this little adjustable focus, 3 aaa, cree led flashlight, and it doesn't do everything the description says it would do, and it has middle of the road brightness (compared to other led lights), I STILL love it. Just like a $3 bottle of Oak Leaf Pinot Grigio from Walmart, for $9.90 this flashlight was nearly guaranteed to please. Admittedly, as long as it didn't short-circuit and cook my fingers like grilled kielbasa, I was probably going to like it. Using only 3 aaa batteries, this thing throws a beam that will make you wonder why you'd want any flashlight that's more powerful (trust me - you will). It will also zoom out and cast a flood that's very impressive. What it DOESN'T do is strobe or change brightness, even though the description says it will. You know what? I'm giving it 5 stars anyway. I do recommend taking it apart and using some di-electric grease (silicone lubricant) on the rubber o-ring where the head slides to zoom in and out. Doing this will make it easier to work the zoom. Go ahead and put some on the threads, too. Bottom line? If you haven't seen what they're doing with flashlights these days, you will absolutely be amazed by this purchase. In fact, for less than ten bucks, you too can begin a life of searching for more lumens/$ and trying to justify/rationalize your every flashlight purchase to yourself, your friends, and your therapist. Do yourself a favor and buy it, then give your old incandescent flashlights to Goodwill, the Salvation Army, your so-called friends, or your judgmental therapist. Now - I'm off to look at the K40 website. Again.

Edit: I see the description has been changed and no longer says it changes brightness or strobes. This flashlight gets used regularly and is still a 5 star purchase.

Edit to my previous Edit: They're claiming again that this light has three brightness level choices. It does not. There is a single brightness with no change in battery consumption. I love the zoom feature, but changing the zoom function does not equate to changing brightness. To clarify, the zoom is a continuous slide from spot to flood - there is no setting for spot, flood, or area (and what the heck is the difference between area and flood, anyway?!?). This thing still gets 5 stars from me, but I wish they'd get a better translator.

Update: Just received my third one. I bought it as a gift for someone who will be hiking in Peru. This, along with an [[ASIN:B00C1KI8Q0 Olight I3S 80 Lumen Cree XP-G2 LED LED Flashlight (Black Body) with 3 X EdisonBright AAA batteries]] (also uses an AAA battery and can clip to the brim of a hat), should provide versatile lighting that only uses one type of easily obtained battery. I'm ordering 2 more for some nephews who are in Scouting. Since theirs might get used infrequently, I'm also ordering [[ASIN:B00AHKUOPY Energizer Advanced Lithium AAA Batteries 6 Pack - EA92BP4F2]] ($8.74 shipped) to guarantee against leakage. In fact, I'd recommend that battery or Eneloops rather than alkalines, especially if the light sees infrequent use.

query: I've been experiencing tendinitis on the outside of my foot after using a metatarsal pad, and a physical therapist introduced me to a board that helps with foot mobility. ori_review:
My physical therapist introduced me to the mobo to treat tendinitis on the outside of my foot. Back story: about a year ago I was diagnosed with metatarsal neuritis, and the podiatrist put a metatarsal pad in my shoe. A couple of months ago the side of my foot started _really_ hurting, especially when getting out of bed in the morning. A (different) podiatrist said that was tendinitis and sent me to PT. I believe that, in my case, the metatarsal pad was causing me to roll my foot to the outside, eventually leading to the tendinitis.

Using the board forces you to really mobilize the ball of your foot. I definitely notice that I am walking much more pronated on that foot than I was before the mobo board. And the tendinitis rarely, if ever, bothers me anymore. I've probably used the board a total of 10 times by now, so I got results extremely quickly.

Eventually I am planning to try getting rid of the metatarsal pad, and see if my new, improved gait keeps my foot happy without it.

Update (3/2022): I've been getting along without the metatarsal pad for a month or two now and so far, so good!

query: I'm looking for a baitcasting reel that can handle heavier setups for fishing in the Florida intracoastal and also serve as a lighter option for surf fishing. Any recommendations would be appreciated!
ori_review:
This is the tried and true Millionaire Classic with new colors and carbon fiber drag.

I bought this to fish as a heavier setup for the Florida intracoastal and light setup for the surf. My main surf reels are Daiwa Sealine x30sha but I wanted something lighter to put on a 9' rod to fish the first trough. I have only caught a few winter bluefish between 11" and 18" so far but the reel handled them easily.

The new color scheme is black and it looks great on the all metal body and the gold spool tensioner. Everything is smooth and the drag adjustment turns nicely.

I can cast 73 yards on a 9' rod, 4 oz sinker, stock greased bearings, and with the line leveler in place. It feels very fast though, and if you cleaned the bearings and removed the line leveler I think you could easily cast over 100. I have my Sealines for long casting though so I'm leaving this as is.

The size is comparable to an Abu Garcia 6000 series. You can see the comparison to my larger reels in the pictures.

The only issue - and this is for all reels with a bar and/or button release (as opposed to clutch switch) - is that you need to use your thumb to roll the spool back a little before you put it into free spool if you are using heavy rigs. Otherwise, it feels to me like you are putting extra strain on the anti reverse.

I did open it up to add extra grease to the main gears but they were already well greased. Looked clean inside.

I've had it to the beach a few times, and with a fresh water rinse afterwards, it seems to be holding up just fine.

Highly recommend.

query: I'm looking for a comfortable and lightweight hammock that comes with an integrated mosquito net. I want to ensure it keeps bugs out while I relax outdoors, especially in areas where mosquito-borne viruses are a concern. It would be great if the hammock is easy to set up and can be used without the netting as well. Can you recommend something that fits these needs?
ori_review:
I originally purchased one of these from Woot, but my wife and I kept arguing over who got to use it so I had to buy a second one. For those that tend to be mosquito bite prone, this thing is a godsend. The first time we brought it with us on vacation, we were staying in a small cabin with no AC and I got a bad cold. It was way too hot in the cabin to rest, and the mosquitos were terrible outside. However, I laid a blanket down in the bottom of the hammock (to prevent mosquitos from biting through the bottom), zipped up the netting, and was able to get the extra sleep I needed without a single bit.

The hammock is comfortable, strong, lightweight, and packs up really small in the integrated stuff sack. It's easy to hang, although it doesn't come with any straps or rope (I use a couple of old nylon webbing belts that I can stuff inside the sack, but you can get fancier straps on Amazon). The netting is held up by can elastic cord that runs through two parallel rows of loops, so you end up with more room inside the mosquito net than in other netted hammocks that only use a single string throw one row of loops. The hammock is designed to be used between two trees, where the width of the trunk separates the two elastic lines that support the net, but you can easily use a short stick to separate them if you're hanging it from a poll or hook. The black netting provides plenty of visibility and airflow, and seems to keep the bugs out. The netting is permanently attached, but if you don't want to use it you can turn the hammock upside down so that the netting hangs below it.

Now that EEE, West Nile, zika, chikungunya, and other mosquito-borne viruses are becoming a larger threat, this hammock is a great way to enjoy the great outdoors without worry.

query: I'm looking for a rope saw that can help me cut high limbs from hardwood trees effectively. I've read that technique is important for getting good results; can you provide tips on how to use it properly to avoid binding and achieve smooth cuts? Also, how can I manage uneven cuts when dealing with larger branches? Any advice would be appreciated!
ori_review: Product worked to cut a 4” limb and a 2” limb of a hardwood tree. Limbs were 20 and 25 ft off the ground. For that alone, 5 stars.  Some reviewers say it cut like butter.  Nonsense. It takes time and effort to figure out the best technique to cut.  The blade has a tendency to catch and so you need to work the blade in different directions and tensions to free it to resume cutting. When the blade is free you can make long strokes. When it binds, all you can do are short strokes. As with any saw, smooth light sawing gets the job done faster than brute force.  Finally, some reviewers mention uneven cuts of big branches. I had same issue.  Solution is to first cut the branch a foot or two from trunk.  Come back and cut the stub.  Definitely more work, but a professional result.

ori_review:
This bar is exactly what it says. 5' long, 1" wide (fits standard plates, NOT 2" OLYMPIC PLATE). Weighed about 12lbs on my scale. Really, I can't imagine getting a better value on this. Went to a few local stores, Walmart, Academy, etc, and couldn't find a place that beat the price. And this is a solid piece of metal, so no one could beat the quality either.

There are a few small things. There were small rough spots on the bar, like other people mentioned, but nothing that felt like it could be a problem during a workout. It looks like it could really comfortable fit 4-6 plates, but given that it claims a max of 250, you probably won't need more than 3.

The spinlock collars do slip a bit, and you'l have to re-tighten them as you exercise. I like doing bicep curls with it, so the swaying motion causes the plates to spin and the collars to start loosening. To address that, I added a small rubber washer before I put the plates on to help keep them more secure, and to add some tension to prevent loosening. I'll be adding photos of that later. This isn't 100% necessary, but the collars spin on so easily that it makes sense they loosen easily too.

FOR EXERCISES:
Seems a little short for bench pressing, so if you're looking to get into serious chest exercises (200lbs+), you might want to look for an 6' Olympic bar instead. But for lighter presses (~150lbs) it should be perfect. It's my favorite to use for bicep curls. Overhead presses for the shoulders are great here too. The only thing I don't 100% recommend: I like doing hip thrusts when I'm working my glutes, but at 1" thin, it does dig into you a bit if you've got it loaded with weights. Otherwise, really versatile given its size.

query: I'm looking for a workout bench that is easy to assemble and feels solid without wobbling. Can you provide tips on how to avoid issues during assembly, like handling the bolts and washers? Also, what should I do if I can't find the allen wrench needed for assembly? Finally, how can I ensure that I don't accidentally stack washers when putting it together? For my workouts with dumbbells, I need something reliable and durable that fits my budget.
ori_review:
The bench assembled easily and feels solid with no wobbling. My first work out with the new bench went well. I'll only work out with dumbbells, so I don't envision any issues in terms of weight loads.

A few recommendations...

1. Be careful when opening the shipping box. The package that contains the bolts and washers had opened in transit. Had I opened the box in the wrong area, it could have been a bear to find the washers after they spilled out. Fortunately, I opened the shipping box on the living room carpet, so it was easy to corral the runaway washers.

2. Do not tighten any of the bolts until you have all of the bolts in and they've begun to thread. You have to jiggle things a bit to get all holes lined up. If you tighten things down ahead of time, you won't be able to jiggle the pieces enough to get all of the bolts threaded.

3. There is an allen wrench provided in the shipment. (It was the only tool I needed to complete the assembly.) At first, I didn't see it and thought I'd have to head to the store to buy a metric allen wrench to tighten the bolts, but as I rummaged through the packaging material, the allen wrench appeared. I'm not sure if it was in the same package as the bolts and washers and had broken free, or if it was free swimming in the box. Anyway, it is there, so keep an eye out for it.

4. The washers tend to cling to one another, so it is easy to put two washers on a bolt and not notice. I ended up thinking I was two washers short as I was ready to put the last two bolts into place. On closer examination, I noticed two of the partially inserted bolts had two washers on them.

For the price and for my purpose, it fits the bill.

Seriously, if you want a good blade for busting up firewood and making shelters, this is it. I also own an RTAK II, but frankly if I were stuck out, I'd kinda prefer this blade, due to the extra thickness.

query: I'm looking for a lightweight helmet that provides good ventilation and comes in multiple sizes for a comfortable fit. I want to ensure it offers protection in case of a fall, but I'm also curious about its design and any potential comfort adjustments. Can you recommend a helmet that meets these needs?

This helmet provides protection on many levels. Not only might it save your life should you take a spill (which happens to everyone eventually), but it will also likely reduce the rate of pregnancy by making you seem a bit...mushroom shaped . This second feature is not unique to this particular helmet, but it might be nice if manufactures would thrust their design teams at the secondary issue beyond impact protection.

Some key features:
* This skull cap comes in several sizes, so you don't have to worry about it being too tight or too loose. The small might even be a good cap for little johnny.

* Veins running through the top allow for good ventilation. Things get a little hotter than if I'm free-riding, but the consequences of an unplanned spill make this brain barrier well worth the trouble.

* Easy to strap on, though the bits that dangle over my lobes hang at a funny angle. I'm not sure why they make the place where the webbing forks naturally sit at 90 degrees to the chinstrap.

* There's a little knub you can reach around to for making fine fit adjustments. It's a little hard discover at first, but once you know where it is you'll want to fiddle around with it for maximum comfort.

* Very light weight. I'm not saying it will feel like it isn't there, but it doesn't get in the way too much either.

I don't want to give Giro the shaft on this review just for the look of the thing, it functions just as its creator intended

Cygolite has made their lights reasonably priced with exceptional performance. When compared to the competition, Cygolite products are difficult to beat.

If cables is an issue, the Trion is the light to own. The other manufacturers do not make any lights this powerful that are self-contained with batteries inside the main housing. Before I purchased the Trion, I bought the Triden X 600. The unit came with a stem mount, and all the essentials to mount the battery to the frame. One problem ... my stem length of 100mm was too short to mount the battery. (Units with higher outputs have larger batteries than those that have 350 lumens or less.) Attaching the unit to my high-end carbon frame didn't make sense. It was never an option being that I have an $8000+ professional road bike. Somehow attaching a battery to such a high-end bike was nothing more than a classless act.

The Trion is very well made. I find it durable and suitable for extreme weather conditions. The documentation could be written better, but all the essential information is enclosed. Exceeding speeds above 25mph, the Trion with its 600 lumens generates enough light to give me plenty of warning to avoid any potholes, glass or any other obstacle that may be hazardous.

I ride my road bike in harsh conditions. The Trion has performed well in temperatures ranging from 5 to 40 degrees. There has been no problems with the battery life in these conditions. This light has exceeded my expectations. It comes highly recommended.

query: I'm looking for brake pads that perform well and offer great value, especially with a focus on the Sintered Metal version. ori_review:
Updated 3/30/2023 for Sintered Metal version
The new compound is fantastic! There were minor things on the Copper-Based that were easy to live with for the performance. First, the brake material was thinner and backing plate was thicker than OEM. Overall they were under 4mm total. You got less mileage. Also, the Copper-Based did take their toll on rotors. My rear stock TR-24 (180-24) rotor lasted just over 2,000 miles before it was approaching the 1.5mm replacement point (1.55mm at thinnest point).

The Sintered Metal have more braking material, a backing plate closer to OEM, and an overall thickness just the tiniest bit over 4mm. Significantly more mileage (over 900 versus 500-600) with all the things we loved about the Copper-Based. The edges do seem a little more brittle, so go easy on wheel changes! Still, I have to say the Sintered Metal are my choice now for this pad form factor.

Full disclosure: I was provided a set (4 pads) of Sintered by Corki when I inquired about the compound change. I have since purchased a set (4 pads) as well.

Original review of Copper-Based:
Purchased the Copper-Based pads to replace A10.11 OEM pads for hyraulic Tektro HD-E 350s on an Ariel Rider Kepler ebike. I had used 0.2mm of the original pads and had enough of their turkey gobbler call when heated up.

These Corki Copper-Based pads perform superbly. No more fade and odd sounds by heat buildup. They bring my 26" x 4" wheels, on 90lbs of bike with super grippy slicks, and 225lbs of me, to a quick, controlled stop from 32mph.

Whisper quiet stopping with no fade. Do not wait to replace cheap OEM pads. Put these in now!

query: I'm considering getting a weight bench for about $40 and am curious about its assembly process and sturdiness. I noticed some reviews mention quality control issues, but I found the assembly straightforward with just a few parts. Is it suitable for light workouts like ab exercises and using light dumbbells? Also, does anyone else experience wobbliness on hard surfaces, and would using a rug help stabilize it? I'm looking for a bench that fits my needs without being overly heavy-duty.
ori_review:
I was a little reluctant based on a few negative reviews, but I thought it was worth giving this a shot for $40. I almost bought the Reebok bench for about twice the price, but decided to roll the dice. I think it will suit my purposes just fine.

Assembly: Instructions weren't much (basically two diagrams of all the extruded parts), but there are basically only 4 parts you have to put together... the two feet, the main frame, and the top of the bench. I'd say I got it together in about 15 minutes and I'm not especially handy.

This is a $40 bench, so I'm guessing the negative reviews are quality control issues, which is not too shocking for something at this price point. All the holes lined up for me and it went together pretty easy. The design for the foot attachments could have been a little easier (tight fit for the wrench).

This is not a heavy duty bench. The first time you pick it up, you'll feel it's crazy light compared to a bench you'd find at a gym. That said, it should be fine for my uses... basically some ab work, work with light dumbbells, split squats, etc. On the positive side of that, the fact that it's light will make it very easy to move out of the way when not in use, but obviously that means it's not as sturdy if you're trying to throw around a bunch of weight on it. I'm rating it as 5 because it's just what I need -- if I bought it planning to use this in a heavy-weight set up, I might rate it lower.
-------
EDIT: One other comment regarding some other reviews: I did notice this is slightly wobbly when I have it directly on my basement floor. I think this is actually due to my basement floor not being level rather than a problem with the bench. I usually have it over a rug and it feels solid there. If it's a bit wobbly directly on a hard surface (concrete, hardwood, laminate), I recommend putting it on a rug or those usual gym squares. I think that would resolve it... I should probably break out a level and see if it's really the floor or the bench that isn't quite level, but keeping it on the rug is working fine for me.

query: I'm looking for grips that can help alleviate hand numbness during long rides on my hybrid bike. I've tried other grips and gloves, but I still experience discomfort after 30-40 minutes. I've heard that the Ergon GP5 grips have a larger hand rest pad and adjustable positions for added comfort. However, I had some issues with installation because the grips seemed to slip on my handlebar. Can you provide advice on how to install them securely without rotation, and if others have had similar experiences with their grip installation? I want to ensure I get the best comfort while riding.
ori_review:
I have a hybrid/comfort bike for exercising in the evenings and weekends. I already have a pair of large hand grips with extended pad; but, still had hand numbness after 15-20 minutes of riding. I upgraded my gloves to OutdoorMaster Half Finger with Shock-absorbing Gel Pad and that got me up to 30-40 minutes before numbness would start to hit. The Ergon GP5 have a larger hand rest pad to spread the pressure and I like the handles to change your hand position for added comfort without sacrificing control of the bike. I'm still playing with the best handle position for comfort; but, I like them a little higher up than in the near horizontal setting.

The handle bar hole on the Ergon grips seemed to be a touch too big or my handle bar is a touch too small in diameter because the Ergon grips slipped on with not a lot off effort and rotated freely once I put my palms on them. I experimented with double wrapping black electrical tape the length of the grips on the handle bar and using hair spray to lubricate the bar/tape (YouTube trick). The grips went on with some resistance and took some effort once the hair spray started to evaporate after a while to adjust for the most comfortable hand/palm angle. I also had to insert the grips all the way to the end where the handle bar ends were near to the Ergon adjustable hand grip hold attaches with the Allen topped screw. If not, the Ergon handles will come loose/off when riding. Because of this, the supplied decorative end caps were too long to insert; but, no-one will notice. I have no grip rotation when riding and the handles are very secured on the ends. You may not have the same issue with your bike like I did.

I even ordered a 2nd pair for the wife's bike because I like the improvement in comfort so much.

query: I'm preparing for a 6-week trip where I'll encounter snow and heavy rain, and I've just applied a waterproofing wax to my leather walking shoes. How can I ensure the wax application is effective for different weather conditions, and what tips do you have for maintaining the waterproofing while on the road?
ori_review:
I haven’t worn my black leather walking shoes in wet weather yet, but the application was EASY and I can’t believe it won’t work. Since my New Balance shoes have lots of seams and a separate tongue, the best they’ll be good for is slush, heavy rain and shallow puddles, but that’s OK.

I’m about to take a 6 week trip, there will be snow showers at high elevations the first 4 days, so this should do fine, both then and if there are heavy rains or polar vortex mischief later in the trip.

I heated the oven to 170 - it won’t heat below that, put each shoe in for 5 minutes, until it was a bit warm, and worked on it. Much more importantly, I put the tube of wax in a tall glass, poured boiling water over it and left it there until I was ready to work on each shoe. Be sure to turn the tube over midway through, so the entire tube has the same consistency.

Basically, I liquified the wax, which made it very easy to apply. Each shoe got 3 solid coats. I then “detailed” the seams with cotton swabs, which forced the excess into the seams while removing what was left, which would have looked whitish. After the wax dried, I buffed each shoe with a shoe shine cloth. No residue and the shoes look great.

For an ultralight packer (carryon for 6 weeks), this seems like the optimal solution. And,if I’m concerned, I can throw the 100gm tube into my TSA “liquids” pouch and apply more while traveling if needed.

I will try to update after I’ve field tested their waterproofing - but, with this much wax, I can’t see how they won’t work pretty well.

query: I'm looking for a pannier set that is suitable for commuting rather than touring. Can anyone provide details on their experience with the Seymour LX panniers, especially regarding their mounting stability, water resistance, and overall usability? I'd also like to know if they have any features for easy access to items like tools or first aid supplies, and if they are better than other models in terms of design and functionality. Additionally, do they come with any external webbing or rain covers?
ori_review:
just to help other people without them having to check the web for the volumes of the various axiom panniers, since i looked them all up i figured i would save you all the trouble:

pannier volumes:
Seymour LX [this set]
1700c" (27.85L) per pair
Seymour DLX 30
1830c" (30L) per pair
Lasalle DLX 45
1830c" (30L) per pair
Cartier DLX 35
2013c" (33L) per pair
Kootenay DLX
2441c" (40L) per pair
Champlain DLX 60
3000c" (49L) per pair

that said, i also own this set and love em. they mount pretty decently to my rear axiom rack as well as my front jim blackburn rack. you have to pull pretty firmly to release the clips, which is good because my last set of panniers kept leaping off.

so far the bottom bungee is holding well. its thinner than the other pannier models bungees, but with repeated removal the bungee like any of them will stretch so you will have to eventually replace it.

the bungee on this model is the same size as the one on the appalachian set, it took a good 3 years of constant removal for those to lose all of their elasticity though but they still hold, they just no longer stretch.

like any non-rubber pannier set these are water RESIS|TANT but by no means water-proof. if you intend on using them in downpours, plan accordingly and either use dry sacks on the inside or buy or make exteriour rain covers.

waterproofing sprays will eventually wear off, which is just a "feature" of waterproofing sprays.

this model is more for a commute than for touring. they have a rear pouch for easy access to first aid, tools, etc and i think its an improvement over the appalachian side mounted pouches which really just make them stick out more. the pouches are also low which is going to keep your weight where it belongs.

like most single clip on panniers these sit about an inch and a half above the rear racks flat area, so while a rear trunk will fit nicely in the middle of the bags, a basket or crate will not.

unlike the appalachian panniers, these are separate pieces that you can either use as just one to suit your needs or together. they also snap together at the handles for carrying when not on the rack.

the only thing i would like to see on these bags is make exteriour webbing like they have on the other models and included rain covers

ori_review:
I wore the Inspire2 for nearly two years and liked it but knew it was near the bottom end of FitBit trackers. I felt it accurately tracked my steps, but I knew the heart rate was WAY off. It would sometimes show 85bpm when I was going at it during a workout and should have been around 125-140.

The first was purely aesthetic. I don't care for huge clock faces, and this one looked perfect for me. There's nothing but smooth edges so it really can't get snagged on anything, either.

Beyond that, I liked the larger display, and the improvement in heart rate accuracy is fantastic. I can't say it's 100% correct, but I've worked out for decades and have a very good feel about where the rate should be, and this tracks with that quite closely.

The color display is also very much appreciated as it was often difficult to read the black & white numbers on the Inspire2.

If you need a solid, middle-of-the-road fitness tracker, and if the thin profile works for you, this is a really sound choice.

query: I'm looking for a lightweight backpack that can comfortably hold about 12lbs of gear. I want to know if this pack has features that allow for good organization, like pockets for a water filter and a toilet kit, while also being durable and waterproof. I'm particularly concerned about the fit and comfort, especially with the hipbelt slipping during use. Can it accommodate a wet tent without issues, and how well does it perform over long distances? Additionally, are the hipbelt pockets designed well enough to hold a phone securely? Any insights on these aspects would be greatly appreciated.
ori_review: My base weight is around 12lbs. or a little less and this pack can't be beaten for that size of a load. I've worn it for a grand total of about 12 miles so far, just trying to dial in the fit and the comfort level, so I won't be able to speak to long-term durability yet, but I'm confident I can provide a solid overview of this pack. Inside the pack, even though the fabric is waterproof, the seams aren't taped so I line it with a trash compactor bag. A sleeping bag, clothes bag, sleeping pad, and puffy jacket fit nicely squeezed into the bottom. I usually carry an Ursack inside a waterproof sea to summit ultrasil bag that includes my food and cook kit just above the other stuff in the middle of the pack. For now, the tent is in the pack next to the food bag, but I imagine I'll have to carry it on the outside after a wet night. What you see in the first picture is the bag packed with all of those items and it fits extremely well. The outside zippered pocket includes my toilet kit and my tent stakes. Behind that front pocket is my ditty bag and a polycryo groundsheet for my tent, as can be seen in the picture. One of the side pockets is a little taller than the others, which is probably where I will keep a wet tent, but both side pockets easily hold 1-liter smart water bottles as shown. You can't see it, but my Katadyn BeFree water filter is in the side pocket with one of the water bottles. The Z-seat nicely sits on the top under the strap and my trowel is on a carabiner hanging off a daisy chain on one side. Arranged this way, the pack is as comfortable as any I've ever worn, including my GG Crown2. I've not fully loaded it down with water but I can't imagine those last few pounds would make much of a difference. The only problem I've run into has been the hipbelt slipping down a bit after a couple of miles, where I have to make an adjustment or cinch or pretty tight to keep it from sliding. I'll update the review once I've gotten a hundred or miles on it and revisit the durability but at the moment it seems like one hell of a tough pack. Oh, and one last thing about the hip belt pockets. They are just barely big enough to fit my iPhone XR, but the zippers are sort of closer to the middle of the pouch than the top. I'm not sure if that is a good thing or bad yet.

query: I'm looking for a bike trainer that provides a workout similar to outdoor riding. I've set it up in my unheated garage and want to know how to best install it, especially regarding the rear axle since my quick-release handle can be tricky. Also, I would appreciate better instructions or an assembly video for guidance. I've noticed that the tensioner doesn't seem effective, and I prefer adjusting difficulty through my bike's gears. Overall, I'm curious about the durability of this trainer after a good initial experience. Can anyone share their thoughts or experiences related to these concerns?
ori_review:
Before I write the cons and pros, here's some context: 70 year old, typically ride 45-75 minutes each day around flat streets of neighborhood when weather permits; median speed: 12 +/- 1 mph. Weather here now has too much ice and snow on roads, so I purchased this trainer. Our house is small, so I set up the trainer in our unheated garage.

Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF): while I have no idea of the durability of the product, it provided a terrific workout that simulated a real bike ride far better than I expected. The "pros" described below far outweighed the 'cons".

Cons (starting with the bad stuff first):
1. Changing rear axle: I hated having to change axles; it was necessary because my quick release handle won't allow the stand to latch. When I was pulling the regular axle out and installing theirs, the wheel and chain slipped, so I had to figure out how to get the chain back on properly. Now I'm hoping that I can just leave this axle on when I return to riding outdoors {manufacturer: that's a question to you].
2. Instructions: Instructions are really not good, just as other reviews have said. It took me quite a while to figure out how to position the roller such that I could mount the bike's axle onto their latching system. Then I had to guess how much to tighten the roller screw. The manufacturer should provide an assembly video that is roughly twice as long and shows each step being performed completely.
3. Tensioner: it's basically worthless. There was no difference between 0-8. I'm probably just going to take it off the handlebars and set it on the ground behind the bike stand.

Pros:
1. Great workout: I was surprised at how closely it felt to riding normally. Even the little bit of wobble made it feel like a real ride. It didn't take me long to figure out which gear(s) to ride in.
2. Noise was not a problem: I wore earbuds with active noise isolation and listened to podcasts and music. I really didn't hear any background noise from the roller. Because I wore earbuds with active noise isolation, any noise generated by the product was utterly negligible.
3. Varied difficulty by changing gears: I didn't need the worthless tensioner as I simply changed gears on my bike to change the level of difficulty of pedaling. Again, this made it seem even more like a real ride.
4. Price can't be beat: given everything on the "pro" side, the price was so low that it made it very worthwhile to take the risk.

TBD: durability... I have no clue how long this product will continue to perform as it did so well on the first ride.

query: I'm looking for a golf swing analyzer that can help me improve my swing while practicing into a net. I need a device that provides detailed feedback like club head speed and can record my swings effectively. I've heard that some devices require hitting a ball to get data, and I'm also interested in how to interpret the data for improvement. Additionally, I want to know if the associated app functions well and if it has any issues, like crashing or not recording swings due to interruptions. Can this product meet those needs?
ori_review:
This is a must-have product if you a lot of hitting into a net, where you can not see the ultimate result of your golf shot. For $150 (the price I paid), this is the best swing analyzing tool you can get before you start looking into launch monitors (good launch monitors START at around $1000!).

The Good
This device is rugged, and simple to use. Simply charge it up, download the app to your smart phone or tablet, pair the SwingTalk to your smart device, and insert into the back of your selected club, making sure the index mark is aligned to the face of your club. The SwingTalk does not get in the way of your swing, and accurately provides a whole host of detail, including the club head speed. The battery lasts long enough for two hours of practice, and the app keeps track of ALL of your swings, separated by date. You can easily go back to any swing on any date and look at a 3D model of your swing.

The Bad
In order to record your swing, you must actually hit a ball; you cannot simply take practice swings and expect to see any data. I suspect this is because it uses the 'feel' of the impact to record data such as the angle of the club head on impact, and from that it calculates a whole host of other data. The other issue with this device is that it doesn't come with any information about how to interpret the data and use it to improve your swing. Fortunately, there are several Youtube videos that actually do this. Just do a search on Youtube for "SwingTalk" and they should be the top or near the top results.

The Ugly
The associated smart phone app is pretty good, but still could use some more work. It crashes on occasion, and if you receive a call or text in the middle of your swing, it will not record the data for that swing. Also, the 3D graphic of your swing is not an accurate representation of your whole swing. Rather, it shows the position of the club head throughout the swing and attempts to extrapolate your body position from that. There is another app that you can download and use with the SwingTalk called the SwingTalkDR for driving range. This app attempts to show how far the ball would travel and in what direction. However, there is basically no documentation on this app, and the data it provides is a rough estimate at best. Still, considering the price and how it works, I wouldn't expect it to be able to replicate the results of a $1000+ launch monitor.

query: I'm looking for an activity band that doesn't require subscription fees and has a long battery life. It would be great if it has features like customizable watch faces, a comfortable design, and options for health monitoring like heart rate and wellness alerts. I'm also curious about its compatibility with music apps and whether I can answer calls on it. Additionally, how accurate is the heart rate monitor, especially if it sometimes shows an elevated rate? Any insights would be appreciated!
ori_review:
The pros are:
NO SUBSCRIPTION FEES!
* Great battery life in default configuration, currently going for 7 days and still has a 25% charge.
* There are warnings in the app about features that will decrease or "greatly" decrease battery life.
* It's sleek, lightweight, and comfortable.
* I like that you can configure the display with a whole library of faces. The built-in one even has sub-configurable display areas (e.g. World Clock, Weather or other at the top).
* The charging cable has a two-pronged connector that is held in place by a magnet and works great.
* The app is full featured and offers lots of different monitoring, notification, and customization options and they seem to be actively adding features.
* Has a "find my phone" feature that you can activate from the band when within Bluetooth range.
* Has a built-in guided breathing wellness feature.
* Has a variety of alerts (wellness, calendar, alarm) that are all configurable.
* Can link with Alexa (have not tried this yet)
A few cons are:
* The charging cable is a bit short (about 2 ft).
* I'm concerned about the accuracy of the heart rate monitor - I occasionally check it and notice an elevated heart rate of ~120bpm when mine is normally down in the low 60s. When I initiate an on-demand check, it appears accurate and reports in the low 60's even though it just showed 120 when first checked.
* I still have not been able to link it to my phone for control of the music app (Spotify).
* There is no ability to answer/talk on calls through the device.
* I do not see a way to link it to your calendar even though it has it's own internal events and notification management.

Overall, for the price, you can hardly beat how inexpensive it is without looking cheap or being featureless. I'll update this review as I wear it more!

query: I'm looking for a high-quality poncho liner that is made in the USA, but I'm concerned about the price. I want to know if the quality justifies the cost, especially compared to cheaper options that I've used before. How do the materials, stitching, and durability compare, and would it be worth it for field use despite being overpriced? Also, are there alternatives to buying new that still meet high standards?
ori_review:
This is a genuine, US made poncho liner, and the quality is top notch. However I do feel that it is way overpriced. It should cost no more than $50-$60. That said, I’ll note the differences between this genuine liner (henceforth referred to as “US” liner) and my USGI industries (made in China) liner (henceforth referred to as “China” liner) so that you can decide if it is worth purchasing for the insane price.
1. The stitching - the stitches on the US liner are closer together (I.e. there are more stitches per inch of fabric) and hence it is stronger and will stand more abuse than the China liner.

2.the trim around the liner perimeter - on the China liner, there is a gap where the trim overlaps itself, large enough to fit a finger or pen into it. This can potentially get snagged on something and result in a tear. On the US liner, wherever the trim overlaps itself the overlap is sewn shut, so there is no chance of it snagging. Also, on the US liner, the stitching that connects the trim to the main blanket is stitched higher up from the edge of the trim than on the China liner. This will prevent the fabric of the trim from coming loose easily. The trim stitching on the China liner is very close to the edge of the trim material.

3. The ropes/tie-outs - on US liner, the tie-outs are made of genuine, gutted milspec paracord. The China liner is made of some kind of synthetic rope material that is obviously not as strong and robust as the paracord and looks like it would easily fray/wear out from heavy use. The bartack stitching used to attach the tie outs to the liner is also more robust and better done on the US liner.

4. The Filling - the US liner has noticeably more filling than the China liner

These are the main differences that I’ve noticed. I wanted a liner that I could trust in the field, so I bit the bullet and bought this, but at home I sleep with my China liner. I’ve had the China liner for less than a year and some of the stitching is already beginning to come out. And that is simply from using it as a blanket on my bed. For home use, the China liner is definitely worth it due to its much lower price tag. If you want a genuine US quality liner for harder use, then you have to decide for yourself if it us worth paying double what the liner is worth. Another option is to buy a used one in good condition. You can get them around $40-$50 if you are Lucky. I hope this review was helpful.
In summary, it is top quality, but extremely overpriced

query: I'm looking for a portable and versatile travel spinning setup that can complement my travel casting setup. I want something that is easy to set up and break down, with good line markers. I've seen that some setups can feel a bit front heavy, so I'm curious if there are ways to balance it out. It's important for me to feel connected to the fish while using it, especially when fishing in various conditions. Can this rod provide good sensitivity to detect bites and handle larger fish? I'm particularly interested in its durability and performance during trips where I can't bring my main setups. Any insights on how it performs overall would be appreciated!
ori_review:
I've been looking for a versatile travel spinning setup to compliment my travel casting setup and this has been on my radar for some time. I took the leap and bought it based on reviews and gave it a true test. I went to a couple of my honey holes and caught some decent sized bass. My initial thought is that this setup and breakdown is a breeze on this rod and the line markers do help line things up. The finish reminds me of my 13 Fishing Omen rod and I love it! It looks like quality!

Make sure to spool your line without line twist because the first eyelet isn't that standard huge guide we're used to and may possibly limit cast distance. It didn't bother me at all and it seems to cast fine for weightless presentations. I was able to cast with control with a bit of practice. Balance wise it is a bit front heavy but it's expected from a telescoping setup. I've seen videos of people putting weights on the back (you can unscrew the butt of the pole and place weights in there) to counterbalance this so I'll give that a try.

While fishing I was able to feel everything from rocks, ledges, grass and stumps. I even felt blue gil nipping at my senko! It's almost comparable to my high end rigs! When I got a fish on (you can feel the bite it's wonderful) I was able to muscle the bass out of vegetation and then I tested the back bone out for boat flipping and durability. It passed those tests with flying colors.

In the end, I highly recommend this rod and will be using it when going on trips where I can't bring my main setups or when I go scout ponds for bass. If anything changes though I'll be sure to update here! I've got 6 months of warranty so I plan to use as much as I can but I'm not worried about this blank failing at all. Can't wait to see how it handles a 4#er!!!

We get the bag out, fluff it a little to let it reach it's maximum "fluff status" and add in the sleeping bag liner(which I'd give 4 stars, needs a way to anchor in at the bag so it doesn't get tangled). The three of us get in to test it out and see how roomy it is.. and might I say.. it's roomy! Granted I'm only 5'8" 165, my wife is only 5'3" 115 and my daughter is only 1 year old but we could fit baby number 2 when it comes and still be comfortable. When the fun is all had, I was mentally prepared to wrestle this sleeping for the next hour to get it back in the bag after reading several reviews stating how difficult it is to get back in. My wife is pregnant so she took care of the insert while I single handedly slew the Mammoth. I folded it in half hot dog style and flattened it to let out the air and kept all the corners together and then I started rolling the sleeping bag using my hands and knees keeping the air out as I rolled. I grabbed the stuff sack it came with and guess what???? It slid right in! 5 minutes...  5 minutes! I was blown away at how easy it was, and I did it myself... I wonder if some of these people on here have ever rolled a sleeping bag before? I wonder if they've even rolled their own socks, I'm sorry for those it took an hour and a half to get this back in the bag, I'm surprised you even found the campsite. The sleeping bag is great, it's comfy and we are excited to try it out this weekend in 32 degree weather. I'll update this if I find that the wild somehow changes the sleeping bag, or perhaps my intelligence. If you are looking for a relatively inexpensive sleeping bag to cuddle with your significant other while in the great outdoors, this a great purchase(car camping only, I would never attempt to backpack with this beast). Please, take a moment and come up with a game plan before attempting, perhaps practice rolling empty garbage bags if you must, it's not that hard.

My last trip was to Central Park where I walked up and down heels, (called roads and bike paths) and up and down some stairs too. It was a great work out. These are perfect for improving your balance. I also noticed after walking for about ten minutes in them that my heart rate was up, I was sweating, and I could feel my inner and outer thigh muscles, glutes, hip flexor muscles and core(Stomach) muscles being engaged and worked. These Kangoo Jumps, force you to stand up straight so that's good for your posture too. You can bounce in them and run in them. I haven't been able to jump up and down in them yet with both feet because the springs are still tight. But I can bounce one leg at a time and run in them without knee pain. I did feel some knee and foot pain after the park, but I over did it that day. I purchased the carry bag for these jumps and it's a large bag. But carrying these jumps for more than a five blocks or so is not IDEAL they are heavy. Over all I'm enjoying them, and I get stopped on the streets constantly by tourist who're curious about them. query: I'm considering purchasing a personal EKG monitor and want to ensure I choose the right variant. I noticed there are two options: a single lead and a 6 lead. ori_review: There are two variants of the Kardia device. A single lead graph, and a 6 lead graph. I opted for the 6 lead Kardia 6L variant. It was more expensive but offers twice the data. Sometimes more data can be the différance between life and death. I want to clarify that the Kardia devices are FDA cleared ONLY TO DETECT Bradycardia, Tachycardia and A-Fib. It DOES NOT detect heart attacks. Anyhow, I recently used my Kardia 6L to record some PVCs I was having, (Skipped Beats). What I had captured is nearly 30 seconds of Bigeminy PVC's. (A regular beat followed by a premature beat). My Kardia device classified my reading as "Unlcassified", yet the data was still useful to present to a cardiologist. I am told not to worry about these Bigeminy beats, but it's hard to do! I follow up with an Echocardiogram and Treadmill test in a few days. I captured this result in single lead mode (two fingers only) as six lead mode  (Two fingers and left leg) is a challenge when laying down in bed trying to capture somthing. This is a MUST BUY!

query: I'm looking for comfortable knee pads that stay in place during long mountain biking rides. I've tried the original Pro-X and Pro-X2 models, but the sizing and fit were inconsistent. The Pro-Rugged seems to have an adjustable strap and better coverage, but how do they compare in terms of warmth and bulkiness during hot rides? Will they conform to my legs over time, and do they maintain comfort throughout extended use?
ori_review:
Over the years, I've owned 3 pair of the original Pro-X, one pair of Pro-X2 and now these Pro-Rugged kneepads.
I'm a Colorado Frontrange based mountain biker, and go between chill afternoon rides with friends to more aggressive back country multi-hour adventures (@iRideDumb, if you're into that type of thing)...
I continue choosing the G-Form kneepads, because I choose to ALWAYS trail ride with kneepads, and the G-Form pads have been comfortable enough and stay in place, so that I barely notice them on my rides.

The original Pro-X seemed to fit small. I choose the XL in order to retain feeling in my legs... They didn't slip, they didn't stretch, and for me they held up really well.

The Pro-X2 seemed to fit larger than the Pro-X. I did one ride with a pair of XL, and while the coverage was better, they slipped down and just didn't fit right for me.

Now to the Pro-Rugged... I ordered size L because of my experience with the Pro-X2, and because these have an adjustable strap at the top.

Sizing-wise, this was the right choice for me! They fit well on my legs, and the strap helps keep 'em in place.
The padding section on the front of the knee is wider and stiffer than the Pro-X... which makes it flare out a little wider than my knee, vs confirming around my knee like the older versions. After 4 rides, they have started loosening up, and I think this will conform more to my leg as they continue to break-in.

Heat-wise, these are slightly warmer in that padding section then the originals. The back of the knee is a mesh fabric, which is lighter than the original, and more breathable... so long hot days, you'll notice 'em more, but only just.

Weight/bulk-wise, these are a little heavier/bulkier than the original... but not super noticeable once you have them on.

All in all, these are a great upgrade from the original Pro-X and Pro-X2. They provide better coverage over the knee, and remain comfortable enough to keep them on the entire time during long warm rides!
